src/sqllens/rule_sets.py:480-486 returns f'{value:.16e}', which is 1 + 16 = 17 significant digits in exponent form. 17 significant digits round-trip any finite IEEE double, so the docstring is correct. A MySQL literal with an exponent (e.g. 5.0000000000000000e-01) is an approximate-value (DOUBLE) literal. Traces: 0.5 gives 5.0000000000000000e-01. -1e-05 gives -1.0000000000000001e-05, which _number (472-477) turns into Neg(Literal). 1e-100 gives 1.0000000000000000e-100. 5e-324 gives 4.9406564584124654e-324, which reads back as the same subnormal. -0.0 gives -0.0000000000000000e+00, i.e. Neg(0e+00), still a zero double. Absolute-claim input, inf/nan: rule_sets.py:193 rejects non-finite floats before _literal (494-495) is reached. This verdict rests on my own reasoning about Python's float formatting and MySQL's literal rules. I did not run MySQL.

docs/internal/database-connectors/rule-sets.md:103 claims renaming (not refusing) colliding names means no CTE name changes whether a statement runs. Traced src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py:815-821: with row rules, _choose_prefix (365-376) collects every identifier in the tree (CTE names included), plus listed table names and every rule's tables, lowercased, and bumps sl<n>_ until none starts with it. So a CTE named sl0_c0 or sl0_anything only moves the prefix to sl1_; no refusal. _rename_ctes (379-402) renames every CTE by id to <prefix>c<n>, so a CTE named after a table a filter reads (or any unlisted/listed name) is never refused or collided. Its only refusal, 'unresolved CTE reference' (397), needs _is_cte_reference true (name in scope.cte_sources) yet no owning CTE found; cte_sources entries are built from CTEs, so the owner is found by name-independent id lookup (394-396). The 'unresolved reference' refusal in _analyze (299) fires for a table that is not a CTE reference, independent of renaming and of any filter-read name. Input traced: CTE named sl0_c0 / sl0_0_0 / the same as a rule table (customers): all run. Caveat: a CTE reference differing from its definition only by letter case is not recognised by the guard's scope analysis, but that is unrelated to renaming and to filter-read names.

docs/external/rule-sets.md:203 says MySQL builds the table's visible rows in full before applying the query's own conditions. Implementation: src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py _rewrite (L591-599) replaces every base-table reference having a row rule with _wrap(table, _scoped_body(...)). _scoped_body (L405-422) builds SELECT <listed cols> FROM name AS alias WHERE <rule> LIMIT 18446744073709551615. The LIMIT blocks derived-table merging and condition pushdown, so any query expression (JOIN ON, select list, WHERE) is evaluated on the materialized visible rows. _wrap (L453-468) moves a parenthesized join's other tables onto the wrapper, outside the derived body, so a join condition cannot reach inside. Absolute-claim input traced: a flat [[rls]] predicate. RlsGuardRunner runs beneath the guard with skip_catalog_views (safety/__init__.py:171-205). apply_rls (rls.py:283-310) walks the scopes, finds the guard's inner Select whose source is the base Table, and AND-appends the configured predicate to that inner WHERE (select.where(..., append=True)). It therefore sits inside the LIMITed body. The outer query's own expressions are not added there, and the [[rls]] predicate is operator-configured, not an expression in the query. A second input, an expression in a JOIN ON or the select list, only reaches the outer scope over the derived table's output. The MySQL materialization behaviour itself is from MySQL semantics, not re-run here; the code's mechanism matches the doc.

guard_spec (src/sqllens/rule_sets.py:685-699) raises RuntimeError for an uncompiled row rule. RuleSetGuardRunner._rewrite (src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py:863-866) catches only KeyError, as claimed. But run_sql (886-893) wraps _rewrite in a broad `except Exception` that logs and raises RuleSetRefusal(KIND_UNCHECKED), so the RuntimeError never reaches the inner runner and the statement is not executed unfiltered (894 is skipped). RuleSetRefusal subclasses UnsafeSqlError (line 200). RefusalRedactingRunner (1002-1004) re-raises RuleSetRefusal as-is. In query_database_impl_with_widgets (src/sqllens/tools/query_database.py:793-800) UnsafeSqlError becomes RuntimeError(str(e)), which is the isError path; any other exception becomes the sanitized internal error (805-810), also isError. So it is a refusal, not an unguarded crash. The claim's 'catches only KeyError' is accurate for _rewrite only; run_sql's fail-closed catch-all is what delivers the property.

Doc line 104 of docs/internal/database-connectors/rule-sets.md says any exception while building or proving the filter is refused 'the same way' (KIND_UNCHECKED), with text naming no table or column. Text part holds: RuleSetRefusal.__init__ (rule_sets.py:203-207) passes only REFUSAL_PREFIX+kind to the exception message, detail (which may name tables) is log-only; RefusalRedactingRunner.run_sql (1002-1004) re-raises RuleSetRefusal unchanged, so str(exc) carries only the kind. A TypeError from _scoped_body/CompiledRule.instantiate is caught by `except Exception` in RuleSetGuardRunner.run_sql (886-893) and becomes RuleSetRefusal(KIND_UNCHECKED); that part holds. Counterexample to 'refused the same way': _rename_ctes (called at 820 during apply_rule_set, before building the filters) raises RuleSetRefusal(KIND_UNSUPPORTED, ...) at 397; run_sql's `except RuleSetRefusal: raise` (879-885) passes it through with KIND_UNSUPPORTED, not KIND_UNCHECKED. Also any other RuleSetRefusal kind raised in the build path is not UNCHECKED. So the absolute 'any exception ... same way' wording is inaccurate; only unexpected non-RuleSetRefusal exceptions and the re-walk refusals map to KIND_UNCHECKED. The path is likely defensive, so impact is wording only.
